blocks.text: **Selection sort** builds the sorted array from the front, one position at a time: find the **smallest** value in the unsorted part, and swap it into the next position. It's how most people sort a handful of cards on a table.

blocks.alt: Selection sort on 64, 25, 12, 22, 11. The first round scans everything and finds the smallest value, 11, at the end, then swaps it with 64 at the front. After the swap the array is 11, 25, 12, 22, 64: the first position is sorted and the rest is still unsorted.

elements.text: find the smallest in the unsorted part; swap it to the front
elements.originalText: find the smallest in the unsorted part; swap it to the front

items: Start with the whole array unsorted. For position `i = 0`, scan from `i` to the end and remember the index of the **smallest** value.
Swap that smallest value into position `i`. Positions `0..i` are now sorted and final.
Repeat for `i = 1, 2, …` until only one value is left — it must be the largest.

blocks.caption: min tracks the smallest value found so far; the swap happens once per round.

blocks.text: Every round scans the whole unsorted part, sorted input or not: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 ≈ n²/2 comparisons, so **O(n²)** in every case. Its one strength is that it makes at most **n − 1 swaps** — useful when writing to memory is much more expensive than reading. Extra space is **O(1)**.

blocks.alt: Best, average and worst: O(n²) time, O(1) space.

items: **Not stable** — the long-distance swap can jump a value over an equal one: sorting `[2a, 2b, 1]` swaps 2a to the end, giving `[1, 2b, 2a]`.
**Not adaptive** — a sorted array costs exactly as much as a shuffled one.

blocks.text: When swaps are costly and n is small. Otherwise insertion sort is better for small arrays, and O(n log n) sorts for everything else. The *find the minimum of the rest* idea, though, is everywhere — it's what a heap makes fast in heap sort.

items: Each round **selects** the smallest unsorted value and swaps it into place.
Always **O(n²)** comparisons but at most **n − 1** swaps; **O(1)** space.
